newsitem.title: USA: Kennedy Space Center opens doors to fans.
newsitem.headline: Kennedy Space Center opens doors to fans.

text.p: The Kennedy Space Centre threw open its doors to the public on Saturday for the first open house in its 30-year history.
Between 30,000 and 40,000 visitors were able to drive along the same road taken by astronauts on launch days right up to the space shuttle Columbia, sitting on Launch Pad 39B.
"I can't believe how old it looks," said Dahlia Marks of Orlando, Florida."
"If I was getting on a Delta jet that looked like that I'm not sure I'd want to."
Columbia made its first flight in 1981 and is the oldest shuttle in the fleet.
The wear and tear from its numerous lift-offs and re-entries was obvious to visitors but is not usually seen in television pictures.
Visitors could drive their cars on the shuttle landing strip and wander about in the mammoth Vehicle Assembly Building (VAB).
The VAB, built in the 1960s to house the Saturn 5 moon rockets, is one of the largest buildings in the world.
Inside the solid fuel booster rockets for space shuttle Atlantis were awaiting the rest of the space plane for assembly.
"I came here as a kid back in the 60s, on a school field trip," said Joe Bronson of Jacksonville. "It was cool then and it's still cool. We met an astronaut then and we met an astronaut today."
For many families it was a chance to show children a piece of history that is too big for a museum.
"Over there, that's where they launched the Saturn 5 moon rockets," Ed Gamble of Fort Lauderdale told his three sons with all the assurance of a seasoned tour guide.
"The Saturn 5 was a lot bigger than the shuttle. It had to be so they could get the payload out of earth orbit and into lunar orbit."
Later, his lecture over, Gamble still sounded like an enthusiastic pitchman for the space programme.
"This is the most important historical site on the planet," he said.

"I think of it like this. What if you could witness the first sea creatures that ever crawled out of the water onto dry land -- that's what this place is. It's where humanity took its most important first steps."
But some people were looking for the future, not the past.
At the Space Station Processing Facility, a newer building where components of the U.S.-Russian space station will be prepared for launch, Tina Gersh was impressed by what she saw.
"I can't wait for the open house on that," she said, pointing to a space station model.
